title: Group B Streptococcus neonatal sepsis: antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule (sialic acid mimicry)
vignette: A 2-day-old boy is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for lethargy and respiratory distress. The patient was born at home via spontaneous vaginal delivery at term gestation to a mother who did not receive routine prenatal care. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F) and pulse is 162/min. Physical examination shows tachypnea and grunting. Blood cultures grow beta-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci in chains that elicit a narrow zone of complete hemolysis on blood agar. Which of the following virulence factors most likely contributed to the development of this patient's current condition?

clues.text: mother who did not receive routine prenatal care
clues.note: Without prenatal care, the mother was not screened/treated for group B Streptococcus colonization, so intrapartum prophylaxis was missed - increasing neonatal risk.

clues.text: beta-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci in chains that elicit a narrow zone of complete hemolysis on blood agar
clues.note: Beta-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci in chains with a NARROW zone of hemolysis = group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) - a major cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis.

whatMatters: Early-onset neonatal sepsis from GROUP B STREPTOCOCCUS (beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains). Its key virulence factor is a POLYSACCHARIDE CAPSULE rich in SIALIC ACID that mimics host 'self' antigens, LIMITING PHAGOCYTOSIS and complement (opsonization). Answer E.
strategy: Identify GBS, then recall its main virulence factor = antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule (sialic acid molecular mimicry). Reject other virulence mechanisms/pathogens: antigenic variation (influenza/Neisseria, not GBS), endotoxin (gram-negative LPS, e.g., E coli), exotoxin (e.g., listeriolysin O of Listeria), and M protein (group A strep - not a common cause of neonatal sepsis).

eliminations.label: Antigenic variation - influenza/Neisseria, not GBS
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: changing surface antigens to evade prior immunity (influenza, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, trypanosomes). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: GBS relies on its capsule, not antigenic variation. ✅ Correct if: recurrent infection from antigen switching.

eliminations.label: Endotoxin - gram-negative LPS
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: lipopolysaccharide of gram-NEGATIVE bacteria (e.g., E coli). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: GBS is gram-POSITIVE and lacks endotoxin. ✅ Correct if: gram-negative neonatal sepsis (E coli).

eliminations.label: Exotoxin - e.g., listeriolysin O (Listeria)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a secreted toxin (e.g., listeriolysin O lets Listeria escape the phagosome). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: GBS's dominant virulence factor is its antiphagocytic capsule, not a pore-forming exotoxin; Listeria is a gram-positive ROD, not a coccus in chains. ✅ Correct if: Listeria (gram-positive rod) neonatal infection.

eliminations.label: M protein - group A strep
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an antiphagocytic surface protein of group A Streptococcus (S pyogenes). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: M protein is a GAS factor; GAS is not a common cause of neonatal sepsis, and GBS uses a capsule. ✅ Correct if: group A strep infection (pharyngitis, rheumatic fever).

reasoning: Beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains (narrow hemolysis) in early neonatal sepsis = group B Streptococcus
GBS is protected by a thick polysaccharide capsule
The capsule's sialic acid residues mimic host 'self,' limiting phagocytosis and complement opsonization
mechanism: GROUP B STREPTOCOCCUS (Streptococcus agalactiae) is a beta-hemolytic, gram-positive coccus in chains and a leading cause of EARLY-ONSET NEONATAL SEPSIS, pneumonia, and meningitis (hours to days after birth). It colonizes the GI/genitourinary tract of ~10-30% of pregnant women; VERTICAL TRANSMISSION occurs during rupture of membranes/vaginal delivery. Universal screening and intrapartum PENICILLIN PROPHYLAXIS for colonized mothers prevent transmission - so a mother without prenatal care (unscreened, untreated) confers higher risk. GBS's principal VIRULENCE factor is a thick POLYSACCHARIDE CAPSULE whose terminal SIALIC ACID residues MIMIC host 'self' epitopes (MOLECULAR MIMICRY). This limits PHAGOCYTOSIS and inhibits complement: sialic acid impairs C3b deposition (opsonophagocytosis) and C5a generation (immune-cell recruitment), allowing the organism to evade innate defenses and disseminate. The distractors are the virulence strategies of other organisms (antigenic variation, gram-negative endotoxin, Listeria exotoxin, group A strep M protein).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Micro > group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae): beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains; early-onset neonatal sepsis/pneumonia/meningitis; polysaccharide (sialic acid) capsule = antiphagocytic (molecular mimicry); intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis; bacitracin resistant, CAMP/hippurate positive.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: GBS neonatal sepsis -> antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule (sialic acid mimicry).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on group B strep, polysaccharide capsule, sialic acid/molecular mimicry, opsonization, or vertical transmission? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Antigenic variation = influenza/Neisseria; endotoxin = gram-negative; exotoxin = Listeria; M protein = group A strep.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: GBS virulence = polysaccharide capsule (sialic acid) limiting phagocytosis; prevent with intrapartum penicillin.

keywords.back: Beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains (S agalactiae)

firstAid.detail: Micro > antigenic variation, endotoxin, exotoxin, M protein.

memoryHook: GBS wraps itself in a sugar 'self' disguise (sialic-acid capsule) so phagocytes and complement leave it alone - capsule is the key virulence factor.
